Let $S\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be an embedded smooth submanifold. Using the
Euclidean inner product, define its **orthogonal normal bundle** by
$$ N^\perp S:=\{(p,v)\in S\times\mathbb R^m:v\perp T_pS\}. $$
Local slice charts and orthogonal projection onto $T_pS$ give this set its
standard smooth rank-$(m-\dim S)$ vector-bundle structure. The **normal
addition map** is
$$ E:N^\perp S\to\mathbb R^m,\qquad E(p,v):=p+v. $$
It restricts on the zero section to the inclusion $S\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^m$
and is the basic model map used to build Euclidean tubular neighbourhoods.

Let $S\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be an embedded smooth submanifold, and let
$E:N^\perp S\to\mathbb R^m$ be its normal addition map. For every $p\in S$ the
differential
$$ dE_{(p,0)}:T_{(p,0)}(N^\perp S)\to T_p\mathbb R^m\cong\mathbb R^m $$
is an isomorphism. Consequently, $E$ is a local diffeomorphism at every point
of the zero section.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open cover of $X$. Then there
is a real $\delta > 0$, a **Lebesgue number** for $\mathcal{U}$, such that every
nonempty $A \subseteq X$ with $\operatorname{diam}(A) < \delta$
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) satisfies $A \subseteq U$ for some
$U \in \mathcal{U}$.

Diameters of nonempty subsets of $X$ are defined because a compact space is
bounded ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]) and a subset of a bounded
set is bounded. No choice principle is used.

Let $A\subseteq X$ carry the subspace topology, and let $i:A\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

A continuous map $r:X\to A$ is a **retraction of $X$ onto $A$** if

$$r\circ i=\operatorname{id}_A,$$

equivalently, if $r(a)=a$ for every $a\in A$. When such an $r$ exists, $A$ is a **retract** of $X$.

The subspace $A$ is a **deformation retract** of $X$ if there are a retraction $r:X\to A$ and a homotopy

$$H:\operatorname{id}_X\simeq_A i\circ r.$$

Thus $H(x,0)=x$, $H(x,1)=i(r(x))$, and $H(a,t)=a$ for all $a\in A$ and $t\in I$ ([[def-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy]]). The pair $(r,H)$ is a **deformation retraction**.

Some sources call the pointwise-fixed condition a *strong deformation retract*. In this library the word *deformation retract* always includes it.

derivations.claim: For each $p\in K$, [F2] supplies a local inverse neighborhood for $E$. Form the set of all tuples consisting of a local trivialization, an open base set $O$ containing its center, and a radius $r>0$ such that $O\times\{v:\|v\|<r\}$ lies in that injectivity neighborhood. These base sets cover $K$. Compactness gives finitely many such tuples whose base sets $O_i$ cover $K$; their recorded radii have a positive finite minimum $r_0$. The tuples are collected as a set of all witnesses and only a finite subfamily is extracted, so no point-indexed choice is used.

Apply [F3] to the finite cover $\{O_i\}$ of the metric space $K$, obtaining $\delta>0$. Choose $0<\varepsilon<\min\{r_0,\delta/3\}$. If $E(p,v)=E(q,w)$ with $\|v\|,\|w\|<\varepsilon$, then $\|p-q\|=\|w-v\|<2\varepsilon<\delta$. Thus $\{p,q\}$ lies in one $O_i$, and both $(p,v)$ and $(q,w)$ lie in the same recorded neighborhood where $E$ is injective; hence $(p,v)=(q,w)$. Every point of the radius-$\varepsilon$ tube also lies in one of those local-diffeomorphism neighborhoods, so the restriction is an injective local diffeomorphism.
An injective local diffeomorphism is open and has smooth local inverses that agree on overlaps. Therefore $E$ is a diffeomorphism onto its open image $N_\varepsilon$, which contains $K$ by [F1].

For $x=E(p,v)\in N_\varepsilon\setminus K$, define $$H_t(x)=E\!\left(p,\frac{(1-t)\|v\|+t\varepsilon}{\|v\|}v\right),\qquad 0\le t\le1,$$ and set $H_t(x)=x$ for $x\notin N_\varepsilon$. The normal coordinates are unique by step 3.1, and the formula approaches the identity at $\|v\|=\varepsilon$, so these clauses paste continuously. It fixes the exterior pointwise and at $t=1$ sends every point in the punctured tube to its radius-$\varepsilon$ boundary. Thus it is a deformation retraction of $\mathbb R^3\setminus K$ onto $\mathbb R^3\setminus N_\varepsilon$. Only finitely many local neighborhoods and a finite minimum were used.

Work with smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere; a knot is a one-component oriented link. A **finite planar code for an oriented knot diagram** consists of finite vertex and edge sets, incidence data, a cyclic order of the four half-edges at every crossing vertex, a pairing of opposite half-edges into the two local branches, an orientation of each edge, and a choice of which branch is over at each crossing. Every other vertex is a bend vertex of valence two. The code includes a finite plane-drawing certificate: rational coordinates for the vertices and bends, and a finite polygonal path for every edge. The certificate must realize the incidences and cyclic orders, have no edge self-intersection, and have pairwise disjoint edge interiors except at the specified bend and crossing vertices; at a crossing the two branches must be transverse. These conditions are checked by finitely many exact segment-intersection tests. Edge orientations must join coherently across each paired branch and each bend vertex, and following the edges through the crossing pairings and the degree-two bend vertices must give one oriented circle. Thus an admissible code represents a connected regular oriented diagram of a single knot. If there are no crossing vertices, the code is one oriented polygonal circle and has one arc. Smooth each bend in a small disk disjoint from all crossings and other edges; the resulting smooth diagram has the same crossing data.

An **under-arc** is a maximal portion of the oriented circle between consecutive points where the knot passes under at a crossing; the over branch is not cut. With no crossings the entire circle is the unique under-arc. A **positive meridian** of an oriented branch is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk, with disk orientation chosen so that the oriented tangent to the branch followed by the disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation of $S^3$. Planarity, incidence, orientation consistency, one-component tracing and the over/under data are input validity conditions; a procedure receiving an invalid finite record must report invalid input rather than repair it. The code stores no algebraic crossing sign: the oriented plane and the direction of the over branch determine which incident under branch is on its left and which is on its right.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be the image of a compact smooth embedded circle, and let $E:N^\perp K\to\mathbb R^3$ be the Euclidean normal-addition map $E(p,v)=p+v$. There is a real $\varepsilon>0$ such that $E$ restricts to a diffeomorphism from $\{(p,v):\|v\|<\varepsilon\}$ onto an open neighborhood $N_\varepsilon$ of $K$. Moreover, $\mathbb R^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto $\mathbb R^3\setminus N_\varepsilon$ by pushing each nonzero normal vector radially to length $\varepsilon$. The construction uses only a finite cover of the compact circle and no choice axiom.

If $A\subset X$ is a CW subcomplex and its inclusion is a homotopy equivalence, then $X$ strongly deformation retracts onto $A$. Moreover, if $(Y,B)$ is a CW pair and $u_0,u_1:B\to Z$ are homotopic, then the adjunction spaces $Z\cup_{u_0}Y$ and $Z\cup_{u_1}Y$ are homotopy equivalent relative to their common subspace $Z$.

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair with $A\ne\varnothing$ and supplied characteristic maps. The ordinary quotient $X/A$ is a CW complex, with one vertex $*$ replacing $A$ and one cell of the same dimension for every cell of $X\setminus A$.

If $A$ admits a contraction $H:A\times I\to A$, $H(-,0)=\mathrm{id}_A$, $H(-,1)=a\in A$, then the quotient map $q:X\to X/A$ is a homotopy equivalence and a weak homotopy equivalence. If $H(a,t)=a$ for every $t$, the constructed inverse and inverse homotopies are based at $a$ and $*$. No choice principle is required; a contraction is one witness, not a family of selected contractions.

If $P\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a polygon, then $\mathbb R^2\setminus P$ has exactly two regions, one bounded and one unbounded, and

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].

Let $Q=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be pointed at $[0]$, and for $r\in\mathbb N$ put

$$W_r:=\bigvee_{j<r}(Q,[0]).$$

Then $\pi_1(W_r,w)$ is the free group on the $r$ standard loops, one traversing each circle summand once. In particular it has rank $r$ ([[def-rank-of-a-finite-rank-free-group]]). For $r=0$, $W_0$ is a point and the basis is empty.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

derivations.claim: Cut out disjoint small underpass intervals, one in each crossing box. The remaining projected arcs are embedded and pairwise disjoint: an interior double point would have an underpassing preimage, which has been removed. Put these arcs at height $1$, their ends in the plane $z=0$, and join each pair of ends of a removed underpass below that plane. This normalization preserves the complement pair. Indeed, inside a crossing box the two branches retain a strict height inequality while their heights interpolate; away from these boxes projection is injective and vertical interpolation cannot introduce intersections. A change of height $d(q)$ on a strand extends to a local ambient map $(q,z)\mapsto(q,z+\chi(z)d(q))$, subdividing the interpolation so that $1+\chi'(z)d(q)>0$. Finitely many disjoint strip charts, smooth cutoffs and parameter subdivisions suffice. Planar bends can likewise be straightened in their disjoint strip charts. All these maps are the identity in a common high collar.

For $c=0$, first compare the actual smooth knot with a polygon, rather than identifying embeddings merely from the code. Its projection is a smooth embedded circle $\gamma$, so the knot is $(\gamma(s),g(s))$. Apply the finite compact-tube construction [F2] to the flat curve $(\gamma(s),0)$: the planar slice of its normal tube is an injective strip $\Psi(s,r)=\gamma(s)+r n(s)$, with $n$ the positive unit planar normal. In this strip the ambient map $(\Psi(s,r),z)\mapsto(\Psi(s,r),z-t\chi(r)g(s))$, with $\chi(0)=1$ and $\chi$ zero near the strip boundary, is a homeomorphism for each $t$ (it is a translation on every vertical fibre), and is the identity outside the strip. It flattens the actual knot. Uniform continuity of the tangent and the finite tube bounds then give a sufficiently fine inscribed polygon: each chord stays in the strip and its projection to the circle is strictly increasing, since its tangent has positive scalar product with the nearby oriented circle tangents. The polygonal projection has one full turn, so it is bijective, and the polygon is the normal graph $r=f(s)$. Choose the subdivision so $\|f\|_\infty\|\chi'\|_\infty<1$. The fibre maps $r\mapsto r+t\chi(r)f(s)$ are strictly increasing homeomorphisms fixing the strip boundary; extended by the identity, they give an ambient planar isotopy carrying $\gamma$ to this polygon. Its product with the identity in $z$ is an ambient three-dimensional isotopy. All subdivisions and bounds use a finite cover and one sufficiently large subdivision number. This relates the actual embedding to the polygon without any later diagram-code supplier.

Here is a precise convenient tunnel model for the normalized knot. In each crossing box choose a small convex polygonal footprint $F_i$ and a convex lower cap $C_i=\{(q,z):q\in F_i,\ h_i(q)\le z\le0\},$ where $h_i$ is piecewise linear, negative inside $F_i$ and zero on its boundary. Take the lower arc to be the two straight segments from its two interior top-face endpoints to one interior point of $C_i$. This replacement of the underpass is realized by vertical interpolation of its negative graph, fixing its endpoints. Each $C_i$ is a product neighborhood of that arc: radial coordinates from the interior vertex identify $C_i$ with a ball; on its boundary send two disjoint disks around the endpoints of a diameter to small disks around the two top endpoints, and extend radially. Such a boundary map is constructed by joining the disk centers by simple polygonal arcs, taking rectangular strips around those arcs, and using affine maps on a finite common triangulation; outside the strips it is the identity. Thus it identifies a standard cylinder core with the two-segment arc and its two end disks with the designated exits. Attach product tubes along the disjoint upper arcs to those exits. The resulting neighborhood $N_*$ has one cap and one upper tube per underpass, joined in the same single cycle as $K$; its coordinates are a disk bundle around $K$, not an assumption about an arbitrary regular neighborhood. Corners and the core bends can be rounded inside disjoint smaller charts; retain the polygonal cap boundary, which is only used topologically.

The polygon's bounded side is supplied by [F6]. Triangulate it by diagonals: at a convex vertex use its neighbor triangle if it contains no other vertex; otherwise join it to a vertex in that triangle farthest from the opposite side. The smaller open triangle contains no intervening vertex, so the diagonal is internal; induction on the vertex count yields a finite triangulation. A leaf of its triangle-adjacency tree is an ear $uvw$, with ear tip $v$ and base $uw$. Remove any collinear vertices before this step. Put $q$ in the interior of $uw$. Choose $z_+=q+(1+\eta)(v-q)$ and $z_-=q-\epsilon(v-q)$, with small positive $\eta,\epsilon$, so the convex quadrilateral $Q=(u,z_+,w,z_-)$ meets the rest of the polygon only at $u,w$. Such bounds exist because the closed ear has no other polygon points, nonadjacent edges have positive separation, and the two remaining incident edges have a positive angle away from the ear; finite determinant and distance comparisons select the bounds. Both $v$ and $q$ are interior to $Q$. Triangulate $Q$ by the fan from $v$. On each fan triangle map its apex $v$ to $v_t=(1-t)v+tq$, fix its two boundary vertices, and interpolate affinely. Since $Q$ is convex and $v_t$ is always interior, the image triangles are a nondegenerate fan partition of the same quadrilateral. The resulting map is therefore injective, surjective and piecewise linear, fixes the whole boundary, and extends by the identity to an ambient plane isotopy. At $t=1$ it sends the two ear edges $uv,vw$ onto $uq,qw$, while fixing all other polygon edges. This is an ambient straightening, not a collapse of a triangle to its base. Inductively remove the ears until a triangle remains. From an interior point of that triangle its boundary has a continuous positive radial-distance function $R(\theta)$; the plane homeomorphism multiplying each ray's radius by $1/R(\theta)$ sends it to a round circle. The products of these plane maps with the identity in $z$ identify the actual knot complement with the round-circle complement.

The model can be compared with the given sufficiently small normal tube without invoking a uniqueness theorem or choice. Make its disk-bundle chart smooth near the core and normalize its differential there to the given normal chart; the required linear change is fibrewise, with the tangential component removed by a change of core parameter. In finitely many charts the two resulting embeddings differ by $O(|v|^2)$, with derivative difference $O(|v|)$. Replace the model chart near $v=0$ by the given one using a radial cutoff supported where $|v|<2\delta$ and equal to one for $|v|\le\delta$. The derivative of the correction is $O(\delta)$; compactness and a finite minimum of the chart injectivity bounds therefore preserve a bundle embedding for small $\delta$. Injectivity between nonadjacent core charts follows from their positive separation. The modified chart equals the given normal chart for $|v|\le\delta$ and retains $N_*$ as its outer boundary. Choose the normal-tube radius $\rho<\delta$. In these product coordinates, replace every fibre radius $r\in[\rho,1]$ by $(1-s)r+s$ and fix the exterior of $N_*$. This is a strong deformation retraction from $E_K$ to $\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N_*$, fixed on its target. It agrees on the outer boundary and never enters the removed radius-$\rho$ tube.

Take a large ball $B_R$ containing $N_*$. Outside it, the homotopy $x\mapsto((1-s)+sR/|x|)x$, with the interior fixed, retracts the exterior to its truncation $X$ in $B_R$. Its outer sphere is retained. Write $A=X\cap\{z\ge0\}$. Below the plane, the exterior is exactly $B=\{(q,z):-\sqrt{R^2-|q|^2}\le z\le h(q)\},$ where $h=h_i$ on $F_i$ and is zero elsewhere; enlarge $R$ so every cap lies above the lower hemisphere. The top plates of the caps belong to $A$ as tube-boundary faces, except for the two exits occupied by upper tubes. Thus $X=A\cup B$ and $A\cap B$ is the equatorial disk with the interiors of the $F_i$ removed. On $B$ use $(q,z)\mapsto(q,(1-s)z+s h(q))$ and on $A$ the identity. These maps agree on the overlap, remain in the indicated vertical intervals, and paste continuously because the two sets are closed in $X$. They fix their target $Y_*=A\cup\bigcup_i D_i,\qquad D_i=\{(q,h_i(q)):q\in F_i\},$ pointwise. This proves the global strong deformation retraction, including the lower region and infinity.

The upper region $A$ is a ball with the neighborhoods of $c$ disjoint boundary-parallel arcs removed. The parallelism disks are the vertical curtains beneath their disjoint projected arcs. Their strip neighborhoods are disjoint. Cutting these strips off the upper half-ball leaves a ball with finitely many boundary indentations: flatten each indentation in its rectangular strip coordinate, fixing the other faces. The strip containing an arc is a ball with a straight diameter tube removed. In cylindrical coordinates this last space is $S^1\times\{(r,z):r\ge\epsilon,\ r^2+z^2\le1\},$ whose second factor is a convex disk. Hence $A$ is a boundary connected sum of $c$ solid tori, glued through specified disks to the remaining ball. For an actual bouquet spine, cut each solid torus across a meridian disk and absorb its remaining ball into the central ball. The result is a central ball with $c$ product one-handles. Join the centers of the $2c$ attaching disks to an interior point by disjoint star arms in that ball; after flattening the finitely many boundary disks, these are radial arms from their centers to the central point. Add the one-handle core intervals. The resulting embedded graph is a bouquet of $c$ circles, since every vertex other than the central one has degree two. To specify the CW structure for the relative contraction, use a finite polyhedral ball model for the central ball. Triangulate its boundary so that each attaching disk is a subcomplex and its center is a vertex, then cone that boundary triangulation to one interior vertex. Each radial star arm is an edge of this cone triangulation. The union $C$ of the attaching disks and these star edges is a finite CW subcomplex. It is contractible by contracting each disk to its center and then the star to the interior vertex. The central ball $B_0$ and $C$ are both nonempty and contractible, so the inclusion $C\hookrightarrow B_0$ is a homotopy equivalence. By [F3], $B_0$ strongly deformation retracts onto $C$, fixing $C$ pointwise; HEP alone is not being used to assert a contraction. Next contract every attaching disk linearly to its center, and contract the transverse disk factor of each product one-handle by the same linear factor. These formulas agree on the end disks and fix the star edges and handle cores, so they paste to a strong deformation retraction onto the stated bouquet. For each drilled arc, orient its graph loop to represent the based positive meridian. In an oriented normal-disk chart along the oriented knot tangent, choose the disk orientation so that tangent followed by disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation, and traverse the disk boundary in its induced positive direction. In the complement product $S^1\times D^2$ of the drilled tube, this boundary is the $S^1$ factor; contracting the disk factor and using the retained collar access path carries it to the corresponding bouquet loop. Thus the chosen generator is the positive meridian, not its inverse. Each such loop crosses precisely its own curtain once. Consequently [F5] identifies these positively oriented meridians as the free basis, rather than merely normal generators.

Fix disk coordinates $\phi_i:\overline D^2\to D_i$ and constants $0<r_0<r_1<1$. In $Y_*$ set $V_i=\phi_i(\{|v|<r_1\})$ and let $U$ be the complement of the union of the closed disks $\phi_i(\{|v|\le r_0\})$. These sets are relative-open: the cap interiors have their ordinary disk topology, their closures away from their boundary are disjoint from $A$, and the omitted closed disks are closed in $Y_*$. They cover because $r_0<r_1$. Each $V_i$ is an open disk, different $V_i$ are disjoint, and their overlaps with $U$ are exactly the annuli $r_0<|v|<r_1$. On each outer collar, increasing its radius by $r\mapsto(1-s)r+s$ retracts $U$ to $A$, fixing $A$. Step 5.1 supplies its meridian basis. Transfer these sets and the composed homotopies back through the finite normalizations in steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1. They give the stated subspace and cover in the original exterior.

For the resulting round circle use $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$, $K=\{z_1=0\}$, and infinity $p=(1,0)$. Choose the angular coordinate so that increasing $t$ gives the positively oriented meridian (replace $t$ by $-t$ if the carried knot orientation requires it). The map $(w,e^{it})\longmapsto(\sqrt{1-|w|^2}e^{it},w)$ identifies $S^3\setminus K$ with $D^\circ\times S^1$, and $p$ with $(0,1)$. Choose a center-preserving homeomorphism from $D^\circ$ to $(-1,1)^2$. For $q\in(-1,1)^2$, put $r=\|q\|_\infty$ and define $$c(q)=\begin{cases}q,&r\le\tfrac12,\\[2pt]q/(2r),&r>\tfrac12.\end{cases}$$ The homotopy $C_s(q)=(1-s)q+sc(q)$ stays in the open square, fixes $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]^2$, and preserves $q=0$. Therefore $(q,z)\mapsto(C_s(q),z)$ is a strong deformation retraction of $(D^\circ\times S^1)\setminus\{(0,1)\}$ onto $([-1/2,1/2]^2\times S^1)\setminus\{(0,1)\}$: when $z=1$, every point in the punctured fiber has $q\ne0$, and $C_s(q)$ is a positive scalar multiple of $q$, so the homotopy never reaches the puncture. Rescaling the square gives $([-1,1]^2\times S^1)\setminus\{(0,1)\}$. Write $S^1=[-1,1]/(-1\sim1)$ with the puncture at circle coordinate $0$. For $v\in[-1,1]^3\setminus\{0\}$, the homotopy $$H_s(v)=\left(1-s+\frac{s}{\|v\|_\infty}\right)v$$ retracts onto the cube boundary, fixes both identified end faces pointwise, and therefore descends to the product quotient. Its image $X_0$ is a finite CW complex: the lateral faces form the torus $T=\partial[-1,1]^2\times S^1$, and the two square end faces become one disk $D^2$ attached along $\ell=\partial[-1,1]^2\times\{1\}$. Give $T$ its product CW structure with $\ell$ as a subcomplex; then $D^2$ is a contractible CW subcomplex of $X_0$. By [F4], collapsing it is a homotopy equivalence, and the quotient is $T$ with $\ell$ collapsed. Cutting $T$ along $\ell$ gives a cylinder; after the two boundary copies of $\ell$ are collapsed to their common point, the quotient is a sphere with its two poles identified. To identify its homotopy type explicitly, let $Z$ be $S^2$ with an interval attached at its two distinct poles. Give $Z$ the finite CW structure in which the interval is a 1-cell and its endpoints are 0-cells, so the interval is a contractible subcomplex. Collapsing it identifies the poles, so [F4] makes $Z$ homotopy equivalent to the sphere-with-poles-identified quotient. The two endpoint maps of the interval into $S^2$ are homotopic along a fixed path; choose this path to be the $e^{it}$ meridian cut at $t=0$. By the attaching-map clause of [F3], $Z$ is homotopy equivalent to the adjunction space with both endpoints attached at one pole, namely $S^2\vee S^1$, and the new circle is the retained positive meridian. For this wedge with wedge point $w$, choose $q\in S^2\setminus\{w\}$ and $r\in S^1\setminus\{w\}$, and set $$A=S^1\cup(S^2\setminus\{q\}),\qquad B'=(S^1\setminus\{r\})\cup S^2.$$ These are open in the wedge topology and cover $S^1\vee S^2$. The first deformation retracts to $S^1$, the second to $S^2$, so both are path-connected; their overlap $(S^1\setminus\{r\})\cup(S^2\setminus\{q\})$ is nonempty and contracts to $w$ by contracting each punctured summand to $w$. Thus the sets and overlap satisfy the path-connected open-cover hypotheses of van Kampen [F5], which gives $\pi_1(S^1\vee S^2,w)\cong\pi_1(S^1,w)*\pi_1(S^2,w)\cong\mathbb Z*1\cong\mathbb Z$, generated by the positive meridian circle. Finally the normal radial homotopy [F2] proves the asserted retraction onto $E_K$ in every case.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a regular diagram represented by a valid finite planar code, and let $c$ be its number of crossings. Choose a sufficiently small closed normal tube $N(K)$ and set $E_K=\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. If $c>0$, there is a subspace $Y\subset E_K$, fixed pointwise by a strong deformation retraction of $E_K$, with a finite relative-open cover
$$Y=U\cup V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_c.$$
The space $U$ deformation retracts to a wedge of $c$ circles. Given $p,q\in U$, choose $r$ in an open ball outside $C_p\cup C_q$, which is possible because that union has outer volume zero. If the segment $[p,r]$ met $K$ at $k(s)$, then $r=p+t(k(s)-p)$ for some $t\ge1$, contrary to $r\notin C_p$; similarly $[q,r]$ misses $K$. The broken line from $p$ to $r$ to $q$ lies in $U$. Since this ball is convex, every based loop contracts to its own basepoint by the straight-line homotopy inside the ball; [F3] therefore makes $V$ simply connected. The same inversion identifies $U\cap V$ with $0<\|y\|<1/R$. Then $r_*i_*$ is the identity, while $i_*r_*$ is an isomorphism: the radial deformation from $\operatorname{id}$ to $i r$ has a basepoint track, and [F7, F8] identify its induced map with the corresponding basepoint-change isomorphism. Hence $r_*$ is an isomorphism. Scaling identifies $S^2_\rho$ with $S^2$, which is simply connected at every basepoint by [F2]; thus [F3] makes $U\cap V$ simply connected.

three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept

Work with smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere; a knot is a one-component oriented link. A **finite planar code for an oriented knot diagram** consists of finite vertex and edge sets, incidence data, a cyclic order of the four half-edges at every crossing vertex, a pairing of opposite half-edges into the two local branches, an orientation of each edge, and a choice of which branch is over at each crossing. Every other vertex is a bend vertex of valence two. The code includes a finite plane-drawing certificate: rational coordinates for the vertices and bends, and a finite polygonal path for every edge. The certificate must realize the incidences and cyclic orders, have no edge self-intersection, and have pairwise disjoint edge interiors except at the specified bend and crossing vertices; at a crossing the two branches must be transverse. These conditions are checked by finitely many exact segment-intersection tests. Edge orientations must join coherently across each paired branch and each bend vertex, and following the edges through the crossing pairings and the degree-two bend vertices must give one oriented circle. Thus an admissible code represents a connected regular oriented diagram of a single knot. If there are no crossing vertices, the code is one oriented polygonal circle and has one arc. Smooth each bend in a small disk disjoint from all crossings and other edges; the resulting smooth diagram has the same crossing data.

An **under-arc** is a maximal portion of the oriented circle between consecutive points where the knot passes under at a crossing; the over branch is not cut. With no crossings the entire circle is the unique under-arc. A **positive meridian** of an oriented branch is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk, with disk orientation chosen so that the oriented tangent to the branch followed by the disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation of $S^3$. Planarity, incidence, orientation consistency, one-component tracing and the over/under data are input validity conditions; a procedure receiving an invalid finite record must report invalid input rather than repair it. The code stores no algebraic crossing sign: the oriented plane and the direction of the over branch determine which incident under branch is on its left and which is on its right.

Define a procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ on a finite planar code $D$ for one oriented knot and a designated under-arc $a_0$ as follows. First check all incidence, valence, branch-pairing, crossing over/under, edge-orientation, and one-component conditions in the code. For each pair of rational line segments in the drawing certificate, compute the determinant of their direction vectors. If it is nonzero, solve the two-coordinate linear intersection equations and check whether the solution lies on both closed segments. If the determinant is zero, test collinearity and overlap by exact rational determinant and endpoint-order comparisons. Accept an intersection only when it is a shared declared bend or crossing vertex with the recorded incidence, and at a crossing verify that the two branch direction vectors have nonzero determinant. Reject self-intersections and all unrecorded intersections. If any check fails, return `invalid-input`. Otherwise traverse the oriented knot once starting at $a_0$, label the maximal under-arcs $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, and introduce one symbol $x_i$ for the positive meridian of each $a_i$. For each crossing $v$, read its oriented over-tangent and positive in-plane normal. Let $a_s$ be the under-side from which that normal points and $a_t$ the side toward which it points, and read the over-arc $a_o$. Append exactly the relator $x_o^{-1}x_sx_ox_t^{-1}$. Equivalently, if the incoming under-tangent follows that normal, append $x_o^{-1}x_{\rm in}x_ox_{\rm out}^{-1}$; otherwise append $x_ox_{\rm in}x_o^{-1}x_{\rm out}^{-1}$. The orientation of a positive meridian is fixed locally by requiring the knot tangent followed by the normal-disk orientation to give the ambient orientation. Once a complement basepoint and basing paths to the meridians are fixed, interpret $x_i$ as the corresponding based positive meridian. Return the finite group presentation with generators $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ and this one relator per crossing.

Orient the projection plane by the viewing normal and the ambient orientation. At an oriented crossing let $o$ be the over-arc, and let $n_o$ be its positive in-plane normal: the ordered pair consisting of the over-tangent and $n_o$ is positive. Call the under-side from which $n_o$ points the source $s$, and the side toward which it points the target $t$. A positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk whose orientation, preceded by the oriented knot tangent, is the ambient orientation. With the common upper-collar basing paths, the based positive meridians satisfy
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_s m_o.$$
This side-based equation is independent of the direction of the understrand. In an oriented chart with over-tangent rightward, the target is the upper side $L$ and source the lower side $R$, so equivalently $m_R=m_o m_Lm_o^{-1}$. In incoming/outgoing notation, the outgoing under-meridian is $m_o^{-1}m_{\rm in}m_o$ if the under-tangent points along $n_o$, and is $m_om_{\rm in}m_o^{-1}$ otherwise. Reversing a chosen meridian loop inverts its class. Changing every common access path by the same based loop conjugates all three classes simultaneously.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $D$ be a valid finite planar code for a regular diagram of $K$, choose a basepoint $b$ in the complement, and designate a starting under-arc. The finite procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ terminates and returns a presentation with one positive-meridian generator for each under-arc and one crossing conjugacy relator for each crossing. For the based meridians determined by the diagram's common upper-collar paths from $b$, the homomorphism from the presented group to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b)$ that sends each generator to its corresponding based positive meridian is an isomorphism. Changing the designated starting under-arc only relabels the same finite cyclic arc set and gives an isomorphic presentation. If all basing paths are changed by prepending the same based loop, every generator image is conjugated by the same element, so the isomorphism type is unchanged.

A **free group on a set $X$** is a group $F(X)$ together with a map
$i:X\to F(X)$ such that, for every group $G$ and every function $u:X\to G$,
there is a unique group homomorphism $\widehat u:F(X)\to G$ satisfying

$$\widehat u\circ i=u.$$

The reduced-word construction supplies such a group; the construction and its
universal property are established in [[thm-reduced-words-form-the-free-group]].
When no ambiguity arises, $x\in X$ is identified with its image $i(x)$.

Let $F(X)$ be a free group and let $R\subseteq F(X)$ be a set of words, called
**relations**. The group with presentation

$$\langle X\mid R\rangle:=F(X)/\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle_{F(X)}$$

is the quotient by the normal closure of $R$. The members of $X$ are its
**generators**. In this quotient, every relation in $R$ becomes the identity,
as do all consequences forced by normality.

derivations.claim: The eight stated routes give 24 segments, 16 degree-two ports and four crossing vertices. Here is an exact reproducible intersection test for the displayed integers. For segments $a+tu,b+sv$, with $u=a'-a,v=b'-b$ and $\Delta=\det(u,v)\ne0$, their intersection parameters are $$t=\det(b-a,v)/\Delta,\qquad s=\det(b-a,u)/\Delta.$$ Retain the intersection just when $0\le t,s\le1$. If $\Delta=0$, the test $\det(b-a,u)=0$ detects collinearity, and comparison of the two closed endpoint intervals in either nonconstant coordinate detects overlap. Applying these formulas to the table gives 276 unordered segment pairs: precisely 40 meet, each solely at its common declared endpoint, and the other 236 are disjoint. The 40 consist of one pair at each of the 16 ports and six pairs at each of the four crossing centers. No pair overlaps in positive length. At each center the $Oi,C,Oo$ and $Ui,C,Uo$ triples are collinear with the center strictly between the ports. The determinants of the full oriented over/under vectors are respectively $-69696,3168,3168,-69696$, so those are transverse opposite pairs with exactly the stated cyclic orders. The cyclic visit list uses every branch once, and following the paired branches gives that single list, not several circles. Hence every validity condition in [F1] holds. Finitely many nonincident compact segments have positive distance, so sufficiently small disjoint bend disks introduce no new crossing; over/under height separation in the crossing disks realizes the smooth knot.

The geometric figure-eight admission can be checked without inferring knot type from a group presentation. Draw the downward three-strand braid with successive crossings $\sigma_1,\sigma_2^{-1},\sigma_1,\sigma_2^{-1}$, where a positive generator has its left strand over, and close corresponding endpoints outside the braid rectangle without additional crossings. Number its successive crossings $1,2,4,3$. Following its first top strand through the closure gives exactly $1O,2U,3O,1U,4O,3U,2O,4U$. In right/up plane coordinates its positive-generator over and under tangents point respectively down-right and down-left, giving negative determinant; the negative generator reverses that sign. Thus the four labeled determinants are $-,+,+,-$. Together with the visit list these determine precisely the cyclic orders in the statement. For an additional check, the six face boundary cycles, listing each departure port and then taking the next counterclockwise port after traversing its edge, are $$(1Oo,2Oo,4Oi),\ (1Ui,3Uo,2Ui),\ (1Oi,4Oo,3Oo),\ (1Uo,4Uo),\ (2Uo,3Ui,4Ui),\ (2Oi,3Oi).$$ These are the same two bigons and four triangular faces of that closed braid drawing; the table merely subdivides its eight edges at their ports. To see that this comparison concerns embeddings, take small crossing disks and narrow edge rectangles in each drawing. The identical cyclic orders identify these neighborhoods respecting over/under pairs. The six face boundaries are simple polygonal circles. Their disk coordinates can be obtained by the elementary finite polygon construction: use the vertical-slab convex-cell triangulation of [F6] and peel boundary triangles to identify the filled polygon with a disk. At each peeling step a triangle with one boundary edge and interior opposite vertex leaves a disk; if all vertices of the remaining triangulation are on its boundary, the dual is a finite tree and a leaf triangle has two boundary edges. Reversing these elementary triangle attachments gives disk coordinates with the prescribed boundary parametrization. Matching the resulting boundary circle coordinates extends over the disk by $(r,z)\mapsto(r,h(z))$. Applying this to each paired face extends the neighborhood identification over every face; the exterior is treated as a disk on the sphere. After rounding, this is the same regular spherical diagram, and choosing the same outer face gives the planar diagram. The closed braid just described is the standard two-clasp four-crossing figure-eight diagram (equivalently its usual alternating closed-three-braid description). This verifies admission by the full embedded diagram, not solely its under-arc relators.

Cutting the oriented visit circle at its four $U$ visits gives the four claimed under-arcs. The intervening $O$ visits put $O1$ on $x_1$, $O3$ on $x_2$, $O4$ on $x_3$, and $O2$ on $x_4$. For a direct side check, let $o_r=rOo-rOi$. The values of $\det(o_r,rUi-C_r)$ are $15840,-2376,-2376,15840$; those of $\det(o_r,rUo-C_r)$ are $-53856,792,792,-53856$. Positive values are the left side. This proves every entry of the crossing table, including which underpass follows the positive normal. By [F2] and [F3], $x_o^{-1}x_Rx_ox_L^{-1}=1$ is equivalently $x_ox_L=x_Rx_o$. Substitution of the four rows gives exactly $R_1,R_2,R_3,R_4$ as displayed. By [F4] these are the actual complement group and positive meridians. Starting at $x_1$ the underpasses are $R_2,R_1,R_3,R_4$ and the corresponding crossing signs sum to $1-1+1-1=0$.

In the group with the first three relators, left-multiply $R_3$ by $x_1$ and then use $R_1$ and $R_2$ to obtain $$x_1x_3x_2=x_1x_2x_4=x_3x_1x_4=x_3x_4x_2.$$ Right cancellation gives $x_1x_3=x_3x_4$, which is precisely $R_4$. Conversely imposing all four imposes the first three, so [F5] gives inverse identity-on-generator quotient maps. Thus deletion of the fourth relator changes neither the group nor the meridian assignment.

The square is a simple crossing-free polygon with coherent counterclockwise orientation and one component, so it is a valid code with a single under-arc and no crossing scan. Rounding it gives the ordinary planar unknot. By [F2] and [F4] its complement group is $\langle x\mid\ \rangle$. Define the homomorphism from this free group to $\mathbb Z$ by $x\mapsto1$, using [F5], and the homomorphism back by $n\mapsto x^n$. Their composites fix the generator and all integers, respectively, and are identities; the first claim also follows from uniqueness in [F5]. This proves the asserted infinite cyclic group on the positive meridian without imposing any nonexistent crossing relator.
